clinical_category: Cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy - nutrition and fasting avoidance
blueprint_topic: Nutrition support and comfort-focused dietary teaching in chronic liver disease
stem: A client with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy is eating poorly because the family believes protein will worsen the encephalopathy. Which nursing teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Do not routinely restrict protein; encourage adequate protein intake with small, frequent meals and a late-evening snack to reduce prolonged fasting and muscle catabolism.
options.B: Restrict protein whenever hepatic encephalopathy is present because dietary protein reliably worsens neurologic symptoms.
options.C: Use prolonged fasting between meals to reduce ammonia production, even if the client is losing muscle mass.
options.D: Avoid nutrition-focused interventions until the encephalopathy has completely resolved because maintaining muscle mass does not affect cirrhosis care.

rationale: A is correct. Current AASLD guidance emphasizes that malnutrition and sarcopenia are common in cirrhosis and that protein should not be routinely restricted in patients with hepatic encephalopathy. AASLD recommends minimizing fasting with small, regularly spaced meals and an early breakfast and/or late-evening high-protein snack to support adequate intake and reduce muscle catabolism. B is incorrect because routine protein restriction is specifically discouraged; historical concern that protein worsens hepatic encephalopathy has not been supported by later evidence. C is incorrect because prolonged fasting promotes catabolism in cirrhosis rather than protecting the client. D is incorrect because nutritional assessment and support are important throughout cirrhosis care, including when hepatic encephalopathy is present. The final item replaces the duplicate fall-risk construct from the source with a distinct Basic Care and Comfort nutrition decision supported by current AASLD guidance.
educational_objective: Teach clients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy to avoid routine protein restriction and prolonged fasting, using adequate protein intake and frequent meals or a late-evening snack to support nutrition and preserve muscle mass.
source_organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
source_document_title: Malnutrition, Frailty, and Sarcopenia in Patients with Cirrhosis; Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis; Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis
source_version_date: AASLD Practice Guidance updated 2021-07 and current on AASLD site; supporting AASLD clinical resources published 2022 and 2024 and accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: AASLD Practice Guidance page 'Malnutrition, Frailty, and Sarcopenia in Patient with Cirrhosis' → current Practice Guidance. AASLD 'Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis' → 'Malnutrition in Cirrhosis': protein intake should not be restricted in hepatic encephalopathy; minimize fasting to 3-4 hour intervals; early breakfast and/or late-night high-protein snack. AASLD 'Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis' → Nutrition Interventions: protein should NOT be restricted in HE; fasting time should be minimized; early breakfast and/or late-evening snack recommended.
source_claim_supported: Current AASLD guidance directly supports avoiding routine protein restriction in hepatic encephalopathy, minimizing prolonged fasting, and using frequent meals and a late-evening snack to maintain nutrition and reduce catabolism in cirrhosis.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Basic Care and Comfort: assess and support client nutrition and hydration, provide nutrition-related care and teaching, and evaluate responses to basic comfort and self-care interventions.
correction_summary: Total rebuild for semantic-duplicate prevention. The source item duplicated the hepatic-encephalopathy fall-risk construct already covered by V2-Q1815. The final item preserves the original Basic Care and Comfort category but replaces the duplicate with a distinct, high-value nutrition construct using current AASLD guidance: do not routinely restrict protein in HE, minimize fasting, and support adequate intake with frequent meals and a late-evening snack.
audit_findings: The source V2-Q1842 was a semantic duplicate of the already approved hepatic-encephalopathy fall-risk item V2-Q1815 and therefore was not retained in its original form.
Fresh AASLD review confirms that protein should not be routinely restricted in hepatic encephalopathy and that malnutrition/sarcopenia are important complications of cirrhosis.
AASLD directly recommends minimizing fasting and using small/frequent meals with an early breakfast and/or late-evening high-protein snack.
The final distractors test obsolete protein restriction, harmful prolonged fasting, and deferral of nutrition care; none is defensible under current guidance.
